title: Design and Run a Real A/B Test
summary: From hypothesis to power analysis to sequential-testing protocol to a defended decision. Production statistics applied to one experiment end-to-end.
contentIntro:
## What you'll build

One complete, defensible A/B test. You will pick a metric, compute the sample size needed to detect a realistic effect, choose a sequential-testing protocol so you can stop early without breaking the math, run a simulated experiment, analyze the results with multiple-testing protections, and defend your final decision in a written report that another statistician would sign off on.

This capstone is the production substrate. ML evaluation in real teams is mostly this exact loop.

## What you'll demonstrate

- You can frame a hypothesis as a testable statistical question.
- You understand power vs Type I error vs Type II error trade-offs.
- You can design a randomization scheme with appropriate stratification.
- You can run sequential testing without inflating Type I error.
- You can interpret confidence intervals in their actual frequentist meaning.
- You can spot and correct for multiple testing.
contentUndergrad:
## Why this capstone

A/B testing is the production-statistics application that ML teams use most. Unlike research-paper-style analysis, A/B tests live under three constraints: (1) you can't peek at results without protections; (2) you need to make a real decision at the end, not just publish a finding; (3) downstream business teams will ask 'what does this mean for revenue / latency / retention'.

By the end you'll have one full A/B-test artifact in your portfolio, defensible against a senior statistician's review.

## Domain

Pick one of the three offered scenarios (or propose your own with author approval):

- **Recommendation system**: testing a new ranking model against the current production model on click-through rate.
- **Onboarding flow**: testing a new signup wizard against the existing one on activation rate.
- **API latency**: testing a new caching layer against the existing on p99 latency.

All three give you a clear primary metric, plausible effect sizes, and a realistic decision context.

## Tools

Python with scipy.stats / statsmodels for the math, matplotlib / seaborn for the visualizations, the platform's runnable code cells for inline analysis. No specific frameworks required — the goal is to prove you can reason about the statistics, not to use a fancy library.

## Pacing

5 weeks at ~3-5 hrs/week. Most of the time is in milestones 1 (setup + power) and 4 (analysis + writeup). Milestones 2-3 are mechanical once the design is right.
contentGrad:
## Notes for the experienced

If you've run A/B tests in production already, the value of this capstone is the **rigor pass**: forcing yourself to write down each decision and defend it. Likely places where production practitioners are sloppy:

- Sequential testing without proper protections (peeking).
- Multiple-testing correction skipped on secondary metrics.
- HTE analysis as p-hacking instead of pre-registration.
- Confidence intervals interpreted Bayesian-style.

The rubric specifically rewards naming when you would have done it differently in a less-rigorous setting and why the rigor matters here.

## Variants

- **Sequential-only variant**: focus the entire capstone on always-valid inference (mSPRT, AVCI). Skip the multiple-testing milestone.
- **HTE-only variant**: focus on heterogeneous treatment effects via causal forests. Skip the sequential-testing milestone.
- **Bayesian variant**: do the same experiment with a Bayesian framing (priors, posterior, decision rule) and compare to the frequentist analysis.

Author approval required for any variant — keep the rubric matching what you actually delivered.

milestones.title: Hypothesis + power analysis
milestones.description:
Pick a scenario. Write down: the null hypothesis, the alternative, the primary metric, the minimum detectable effect (MDE) you care about, the desired Type I error rate (α), and the desired power (1 - β). Compute the required sample size per arm. Document why the MDE you chose is the minimum effect that would change the business decision.

**Deliverables**: a `hypothesis.md` writeup + a Python notebook computing the sample size with the math shown. Include a sensitivity table showing sample size at α ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.1} × power ∈ {0.7, 0.8, 0.9}.

Penalize MDEs that are clearly chasing what's detectable rather than what matters."}

milestones.title: Randomization + stratification design
milestones.description:
Design the randomization scheme. Pick a stratification variable (or argue why no stratification is needed). Implement randomization in code that's robust to user duplicates, returning visitors, and cohort-effects. Document any deliberately broken assumptions (e.g., 'we randomize at signup time, so existing users see a single arm').

**Deliverables**: `randomization.py` + a writeup explaining the design + a simulation showing the randomization produces balanced arms across the chosen strata.

Does the simulation actually verify balance across strata? Are the diagnostics meaningful (not just 'mean is similar')?"}],"passingScore":0.6}

milestones.title: Sequential-testing protocol
milestones.description:
Pick a sequential-testing approach: classical group sequential (O'Brien-Fleming, Pocock), always-valid (mSPRT, AVCI), or fixed-horizon (no peeking). Defend the choice. Implement the stopping rule. Simulate 1000 experiments under both null and alternative; verify the actual Type I error matches the nominal α.

**Deliverables**: `sequential_protocol.py` + a writeup defending the choice + a simulation report showing the empirical Type I error matches the nominal rate.

Are the trade-offs (decision speed vs analytical complexity) named?"},{"id":"correct-implementation","weight":0.3,"description":"Stopping rule correctly implemented","aiPrompt":"Score 0-1. Does the code correctly compute the stopping boundary at each interim look? Are the inputs (interim n, prior looks) handled correctly?"},{"id":"empirical-validation","weight":0.3,"description":"Simulated Type I error matches nominal","aiPrompt":"Score 0-1. Does the simulation show the empirical false-positive rate is close to α? Is the simulation realistic (enough trials, realistic distribution)?"}],"passingScore":0.6}

milestones.title: Run + analyze the simulated experiment
milestones.description:
Use a synthetic data generator (provided in the seed) to simulate users entering the experiment over 4 simulated weeks. Apply your sequential-testing protocol; stop when the rule says stop. Analyze the results: point estimate, confidence interval, p-value (with appropriate adjustment), and per-segment HTE analysis on at least 2 secondary segments (correcting for multiple testing).

**Deliverables**: `analysis.ipynb` + plots of the test statistic over time + a results table + per-segment HTE analysis with multiple-testing protection.

milestones.title: Decision + writeup
milestones.description:
Write the final decision report. Recommend ship / don't-ship / extend-the-test. Defend the recommendation against an explicit list of alternative interpretations. Include: what would have changed your mind, what risks remain, what you'd monitor post-launch.

The writeup is the artifact that goes in your portfolio. Treat it as something a senior statistician would review.

**Deliverables**: `decision-report.md` (~1500 words) covering all of the above + a one-paragraph executive summary.
